highlights.text: a single core sense: the lightness of a thing in the air
الطَّيْر (al-ṭayr, "birds") is the plural of طَائِر (ṭāʾir, "flyer")
Qur'anic shāhid: al-Insān 76:7, a day whose evil is مُسْتَطِير ("widespread")
a verse "so we flew/darted to them with horse-troops and spears."
a single core sense: a thing’s passing away and its failure to last
Satan is called al-bāṭil (“the false one”) because his deeds have no reality
The proverb “mukrahun akhūka lā baṭal” (“Your brother is coerced, not a hero”)
a single core idea: the opening or commencement of a thing
بَدَأَ / ابْتَدَأَ = to begin, commence (from ibtidāʾ)
Qur'anic examples: 85:13 "He originates and restores," and 29:20 "how He began creation."
Cited from the poet ʿAbīd: "neither a wonder nor a marvel."
its words don't reduce to one analogical core meaning
**فَنِيَ يَفْنَى فَنَاءً** — to perish, come to an end
the speaker makes his companion stand and sit by turns, "just as a leader humors a headstrong mount."
single idea is the opposite of catching up with something and reaching it
the thing got away from him, he failed to attain it
the two things grew far apart, i.e. neither one reached the other
هُوَ مِنِّي فَوْتَ الرُّمْحِ — "he is a spear's remove from me."
one sound, single-sense root meaning "darkness"
ghaṭasha al-layl simply means "the night grew dark."
describing a night crossing of a landmark-less desert (yahmāʾ), "dark-at-night" (ghaṭshā)
One sound root: a lowering/dipping in a thing, combined with a sense of overlapping/enclosure.
ghammaḍa/aghmaḍa ʿaynahu — to close one's eye (two equivalent verb forms)
illustrated with a line of poetry by Abū al-Najm
one root meaning (aṣl wāḥid) with two sides: breaking, or cutting
He cites Q 21:58, "so he made them judhādh, except a great one of theirs"
From this he takes Q 11:108, ʿaṭāʾan ghayra majdhūdhin, "a gift not cut off"
A verse of al-Hudhalī speaks of "the masāḥin grating over the judhādh"
al-Jidāl (disputation): an exchange or negotiation carried on through contention, each side trying to overcome the other.
The verb (jādala / yujādilu) and noun (jidāl / jadal) recur throughout the Qurʾān in the sense of disputing or arguing
(1) cutting through or crossing something, and (2) the middle of something
جُزْتُ الْمَوْضِع = I travelled through a place.
Imruʾ al-Qays): "when we had passed beyond the open ground of the encampment,"
Aws ibn Maghrāʾ): "until it is said: let the family of Ṣafwān pass"
derives ل-ح-ن (l-ḥ-n) from two distinct bases
*Al-laḥn* also means the underlying drift or gist of speech (its implied sense rather than its plain wording)
a ḥadīth: "Perhaps some of you is more skillful (alḥan) in arguing his case than another"
treats l-d-d as two sound roots: one meaning disputation, the other a side or flank
al-ladad is intense contentiousness.

highlights.text: Ibn Aḥmar: "I drank the shukāʿā and took doses of ladūd, and brought the cautery-irons to the mouths of the veins."
picking something up off the ground, typically encountered by chance rather than deliberately sought
al-iltiqāṭ — happening upon something by chance
The proverb "for every stray word there's a picker-up" means any notable remark finds someone to hear and spread it.
*Mayl* is deviation from the middle toward one side or the other — going off-centre.
**مِلْتُ إلى (miltu ilā, "I inclined toward") = to side with, support, assist someone.**
**مِلْتُ عليه (miltu ʿalayhi, "I inclined against") = to bear down hard on someone, press against him.**
*Nadm* and *nadāma* mean regret: the grieving distress a person feels when his view of something changes after the matter is already past and cannot be undone
He cites two passages, both using the participle *nādimīn* with the verb *aṣbaḥa* ("came to be")
one sound root meaning the undoing or unravelling of something (nakth)
نَقَضْتُ الْحَبْلَ وَالْبِنَاءَ — "I untwisted the rope and pulled down the building."
Breaking a compact: نَقْضُ الْعَهْدِ is from the same sense of undoing.
a single sound root whose core idea is inertness and the stilling of movement
نَوْم (nawm) is the primary derivative: نَامَ / يَنَامُ (nāma / yanāmu, "to sleep")
النَّيْل (al-nayl): what a person attains or reaches with his hand.
Qur'anic citations: "You will never attain piety" (3:92); "nor do they attain from an enemy any attainment" (9:120)
A poet's line — "I grew anxious, and that is not the nawāl" — is glossed as "not the right course."
settling a matter firmly, perfecting it, and carrying it through to its proper end
he glosses qaḍāhunna as "He made firm / perfected their creation."
A verse of Abū Dhuʾayb uses qaḍāhumā of two coats of mail "fashioned"
al-Ḥārith ibn Ḥilliza, where spears whose points are "al-qaḍāʾ"
al-qilā = intense hatred, aversion. The verb is qalāhu, "he hated him."
93:3 — mā waddaʿaka rabbuka wa-mā qalā, "your Lord has not forsaken you, nor is He displeased [with you]."
26:168 — innī liʿamalikum min al-qālīn, "I am, toward your deeds, among those who hate [you]."
a drinker raising his head at the moment of drinking water
**al-qāmiḥ (القَامِحُ)** — a camel that raises its head while drinking, refusing to drink
comparing lowered gazes to qimāḥ camels
an Arabic expression for the harshest stretch of winter cold
**"A qamṭarīr day."** Describes a day on which evil is widespread/rife (fāshī l-sharr).
verse by Abū Ṭālib about returning a blow measure for measure
A verse by al-Khansāʾ is cited describing stones piled up (muqmiṭirrāt)
finds two base meanings under ر-ه-و (rahawa)
al-rahw = the calm, still sea.
supported by two lines of poetry: one about nursing women retreating to a rahwa out of fear (i.e., to high ground), another describing a bird perched atop a rahwa
A hadith about the tribe Ghaṭafān calls it "a rahwa that gushes forth water"
a way in or opening into a thing, such as a hole
al-samm or al-summ is a hole in something, as in the Qur'an's "until the camel passes into the eye (samm) of the needle"
al-samūm is the hot wind, because it too penetrates bodies with force.
The Arabs ask, "How are the sāmma and the ʿāmma?"
one underlying idea combining beauty, radiance/light, and clarity/purity.
The phrase zahrat ad-dunya means "the beauty/splendor of the world (worldly life)."
a hadith in which the Prophet tells Abu Qatada, about a vessel he had given him: izdahir bihi fa-inna lahu sha'nan
